metadata.title: Is Lighter Still The Best Bet On Robinhood Scaling Onchain Derivatives?

content.text:
When Robinhood unveiled plans to bring perpetual futures trading to its U.S. customers through its own derivatives business and Bitstamp, it raised an uncomfortable question for one of its most prominent decentralized finance partners: Where does that leave Lighter?
The announcement at Robinhood's September Summit put the brokerage on a path to offer U.S. investors leveraged exposure to cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. But rather than tapping Lighter, the decentralized exchange already powering perpetual futures inside Robinhood Wallet for eligible international customers, Robinhood chose to build its domestic offering around the centralized exchange it acquired last year.
For investors betting on Lighter's ability to become a major beneficiary of Robinhood's push into onchain finance, the distinction was significant. Lighter's native token, LIT, fell sharply following the announcement as traders questioned whether the partnership would translate into the kind of distribution opportunity many had anticipated.
But Lighter founder and CEO Vladimir Novakovski argues that the market may be getting ahead of itself. In an interview with Coinage, Novakovski suggested that Robinhood's decision to use Bitstamp reflects the limitations of the current regulatory environment rather than any retreat from its broader decentralized finance ambitions.
"Until onchain perps have regulatory approval, they're not just going to plug that in," Novakovski told Coinage. "There was never going to be a sequence of events where that happens before CFTC action."
In the meantime, Novakovski sees little reason for Robinhood to leave its existing infrastructure on the sidelines.
"They have this asset in Bitstamp, they might as well use it, right?" he said. "But as soon as decentralized onchain perps are possible in the US, that'll be something that will be integrated in one or more different ways."
It's a distinction that could prove critical to Lighter's future. Robinhood may be taking a centralized route to bring perpetual futures to American traders today, but Novakovski is betting that the next phase of the company's expansion will look very different. The question is whether Lighter can position itself as the infrastructure that makes that transition possible.
The relationship is already more substantial than a speculative partnership. Robinhood Ventures participated in Lighter's $68 million funding round announced last year, which valued the decentralized exchange at $1.5 billion. And when Robinhood launched its public blockchain mainnet in July, Lighter was among the partners helping expand what users could trade onchain.
Through Robinhood Wallet, eligible customers in supported jurisdictions can already access Lighter's perpetual futures markets, while Robinhood's tokenized stock initiative is designed to make traditionally illiquid or restricted trading opportunities available around the clock. The combination reflects a broader ambition to transform Robinhood from a brokerage offering conventional financial products into a platform capable of supporting nearly any asset on blockchain-based infrastructure.
That opportunity goes well beyond allowing customers to speculate on cryptocurrency prices.
Novakovski pointed to tokenized stocks as an example of how onchain markets could fundamentally change the economics of trading. Rather than simply representing shares digitally, tokenized assets could serve as collateral for other financial products, potentially allowing investors to deploy their capital more efficiently.
"We support those as collateral," he said of Robinhood's tokenized stocks. "If you have tokenized stocks collateral, you can actually trade the perp in a much more capital efficient way."
For Robinhood, that opens the door to a very different kind of brokerage experience. A customer could theoretically hold tokenized equities while using those assets to support positions in other markets, without necessarily needing to liquidate an existing investment. It's a vision of more interconnected financial products that could eventually make today's fragmented brokerage accounts look outdated.
But whether that opportunity translates into a meaningful business for Lighter still depends on clearing some significant hurdles.
Novakovski said the company has been working closely with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to pursue the licenses needed to operate its decentralized exchange infrastructure in the United States. That process requires demonstrating how a verifiable, blockchain-based trading system can satisfy regulatory principles originally developed for more conventional financial intermediaries.
"We want to do things the right way," he said, describing an approach that involves going "through the front door" to secure the necessary licenses and satisfy the regulator's requirements.
The company believes that groundwork could eventually distinguish it from other decentralized derivatives platforms competing for institutional business. While exchanges such as Hyperliquid have helped demonstrate enormous demand for perpetual futures trading outside traditional financial venues, Lighter has emphasized execution speed, low transaction costs, and verifiable settlement on Ethereum as key parts of its strategy.
"When we started building Lighter, we had the goals in mind of low cost, low latency, verifiable, secure and composable," Novakovski said. "Those are the things institutions care about. Those are the things that regulators care about as well."
This week, NYSE parent company Intercontinental Exchange announced it was investing in a key Hyperliquid tokenization partner, TradeXYZ. That news seemingly alerted investors to how serious the acceleration in perpetual future infrastructure and onchain trading has become. Hyperliquid's token advanced 15% this week after the news.
"The TradFi players are ... fully bought in to blockchain and tokenization and new forms of derivatives, like perps," Novakovski said. "It's very much front and center for them."
Novakovski also pointed to the company's expanding relationships with established financial institutions. Lighter has announced a partnership with Bitwise, and its founder said additional conversations with financial firms were already underway.
"There are other conversations with them and others," he said. "Some are pretty far along. So we'll have more to say on that, you know, in the coming months."
